Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
Any form of physical contact with others
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.explanation: The profile is for a 61-year-old bus driver who witnessed trauma. 'Bicycle' as a trigger is not impossible, but in combination with the rest of the profile it points toward a very specific accident scenario that is not supported elsewhere in the report. The other items emphasize guilt, sensory reliving, and contamination/interpersonal avoidance, creating a mixed picture that is hard to unify around a single witnessed-trauma account.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Feeling 'dirty or contaminated' is much more characteristic of sexual or contact-based interpersonal trauma than of witnessed trauma. For a witnessed-trauma formulation, this appraisal is difficult to reconcile unless there was direct bodily involvement, which is not reflected elsewhere.

Avoiding sex is hard to explain from the rest of this profile. The selected memory and appraisal items center on reliving and guilt about inaction, but do not support a coherent mechanism for sexual avoidance in a witnessed-trauma case.

vignette: Elena had spent twenty-two years driving the 42 route through the eastern corridors, accustomed to the rhythm of traffic and the familiar weight of the steering wheel. That changed on a rainy Tuesday when a sedan lost traction at the intersection of Elm and Fourth. From her bus seat, she watched the vehicle skid sideways, strike a concrete pillar, and flip into the crosswalk. The impact echoed through her cabin before the crumpled metal even settled. When she stepped out, the sight of pooled blood spreading across the asphalt seized her throat. She had rushed toward the wreckage, but other responders arrived first, leaving her standing there as she watched the paramedics extract two bodies. The visual cues of blood and the sudden lack of control did not merely remind her of that day; they directly fed into a conviction that she had failed to protect those strangers and would never forgive herself for not doing more. Because the memory felt present rather than past, she began to interpret her own survival as a moral failure, the thought that she should have protected others and would never forgive herself becoming a constant lens through which she viewed her life. Over the following months, these negative appraisals actively reshaped how the trauma returned and how she coped. Her belief that she had failed to protect others and would never forgive herself actively pulled the memory back to the forefront of her mind, while her conviction that her life was not worth living anymore sharpened her threat monitoring, making ordinary sounds like screeching brakes or the sight of dark stains feel immediately dangerous. These appraisals dictated her avoidance behaviours. Believing her life was not worth living anymore, she began performing quiet mental rituals whenever she felt the urge to look away from a hospital window or pass a salvage yard. She repeated specific prayers and counted breaths in her head, convinced that if she stopped, another accident would be her fault. Yet the rituals offered only temporary relief. Once the mental counting ended, the memory surged back with renewed intensity, pulling her fully into the full sensory reliving of the wreckage—the smell of burnt rubber, the sound of tearing metal, the cold air against her face. Other times, the memory arrived without a clear image, yet the emotion without image crashed over her all at once, confirming her fear that she was fundamentally broken. Because the memory felt present rather than past, she interpreted her survival as a moral failure, which led directly to her refusal to be touched by her husband and her avoidance of grief reminders. When the crash imagery of cars hitting surfaced while she was navigating her route, her hands tightened on the wheel, and the fear that she could not stop something terrible from happening again took root. The avoidance of familiar landmarks meant that every time she encountered a pedestrian crossing the street or the side mirror caught a glint of sunlight on wet pavement, the lack of control she had felt that night resurfaced, reinforcing the negative appraisal that she had failed to protect others. Driving the bus became a daily ordeal of suppressed panic. When a passenger bumped her arm in the aisle, she would step back sharply, her skin prickling with the memory of the crash. Her supervisor had pulled her for increasingly erratic braking patterns near the Elm Street intersection, noting that she would sometimes slam on the brakes at the mere sight of a fender-bent car in traffic. By the third year, the cycle had fractured her daily life and her marriage. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment on a Sunday morning when her husband tried to place a hand on her shoulder to offer comfort. She flinched violently, knocking his arm away, and realized she had spent so long performing silent prayers and avoiding every possible reminder of loss that she had stopped living altogether. She came to the clinic hoping to quiet the relentless memory of the crash and the crushing certainty that she had failed, not knowing if she could still learn to trust her own hands or her own life.
